gap: No result ChatGPT got that I could open states that the 1,536 Wh on the label is pack energy rather than what the AC outlets deliver: about 1,306 Wh using the 0.85 factor willitrunpower.com itself prints, or about 1,382 Wh at the 90% The Solar Lab reports for the Pecron E1500LFP. The only station I could verify at 1,536 Wh near the budget is that Pecron, at $549, so a shopper who needs 1,500 Wh at the outlet cannot get it under $500.
standout_why: I could only open one of the rival pages: willitrunpower.com/guides/best-power-station-under-500/ (in the results, not cited). It already prints the mechanism as a formula, 'Runtime = Wh × 0.85 ÷ (load + 15 W inverter draw)', but lists nothing above 1,152 Wh and never converts a 1,536 Wh label into delivered Wh. The three cited pages (powerstationranking.com/best-under-500/ and the two outletpicks.com under-500 URLs) and runtimewise.com failed to load with a certificate error on every attempt, so I cannot say whether they carry it. The score is 1 because a retrieved rival has the derating factor; the new part is only the arithmetic applied to the 1,536 Wh class and the named 90% figure for the E1500LFP.
decides: It confirms the pick rather than changing it. The Pecron E1500LFP (1,536 Wh, $549 at pecron.com today) delivers roughly 1,306–1,382 Wh at the outlets, against about 979 Wh for the $499 BLUETTI AC180 at the same 0.85 factor, so the extra $50 buys about a third more delivered energy. BLUETTI's own page also shows the AC180 out of stock until late November. It also tells the shopper the plan fails if '1500Wh' means energy at the outlet: that needs about 1,765 Wh rated at 0.85 (about 1,667 Wh at 0.90), and the 1,536 Wh stations I could price today start at $549. I could not verify ChatGPT's $449.99 DYNESS 1536Wh at all.
